input.text: Deep in Fangshan district, southwest of Beijing, Yunju Temple guards one of the strangest and greatest undertakings in religious history: the stone sutras — Buddhist scriptures carved onto stone slabs, generation after generation, for a thousand years. A monk named Jingwan began the project in the Sui era, fearing the faith's texts would burn as others had; his successors continued until the Ming, carving more than fourteen thousand stone slabs and storing them in mountain vaults and a tower of buried scriptures. The result: the world's largest library carved in stone, sometimes called "the Dunhuang of Beijing." The temple also keeps relics said to include Buddhist sarira. It's two hours from the city — the farthest spot in this guide — but scripture-readers, print-lovers, and pilgrims of persistence call it Beijing's most moving museum. The stones have outlasted ten dynasties. Your train ride will feel brief.
